name: Go
year_note: Design began at Google on 21 September 2007; Go was released as an open-source project on 10 November 2009. Go 1.0, which came with a compatibility promise for Go 1 programs, followed on 28 March 2012.
tagline: Google's small, fast-compiling systems language: C-like syntax, garbage collection, and concurrency built on goroutines and channels.
summary: Go is a statically typed, garbage-collected language compiled to native code, designed at Google for large networked programs running on multicore machines. It pairs C-like syntax and performance with fast builds, implicitly satisfied interfaces, and built-in CSP-style concurrency through goroutines and channels. Its deliberate minimalism (no inheritance, no exceptions, generics only since 2022) and its opinionated tooling made it a common choice for servers and cloud infrastructure such as Docker and Kubernetes.
history:
Robert Griesemer, Rob Pike and Ken Thompson began sketching a new language on a whiteboard at Google on 21 September 2007, motivated by slow builds, tangled dependencies and the complexity of C++ in Google's large server codebases. By January 2008 Thompson had a prototype compiler that generated C; Ian Lance Taylor independently started a GCC front end (gccgo) from the draft specification, and Russ Cox joined late that year. Go became a public open-source project on 10 November 2009.

In the authors' words Go is "mostly in the C family (basic syntax), with significant input from the Pascal/Modula/Oberon family (declarations, packages), plus some ideas from languages inspired by Tony Hoare's CSP, such as Newsqueak and Limbo (concurrency)" — Bell Labs languages that Pike had created or worked on. Go 1.0 (March 2012) froze the language under a compatibility promise. The toolchain was rewritten from C into Go for Go 1.5 (2015), modules replaced GOPATH-based dependency management starting with Go 1.11 (2018), and after a decade of debate type parameters (generics) arrived in Go 1.18 in March 2022, followed by range-over-function iterators in Go 1.23 (2024) and generic methods in Go 1.27 (2026).
innovations: Goroutines and channels: CSP-style concurrency built into a mainstream compiled language, with a runtime that multiplexes cheap goroutines onto OS threads
Interfaces satisfied implicitly by method sets — structural typing checked at compile time in an otherwise nominal type system
Fast compilation as an explicit design goal, via a dependency-conscious package and import model
Opinionated built-in tooling: gofmt's single canonical formatting, go test, go vet and a module system shipped with the compiler
Errors as ordinary values returned alongside results (multiple return values) instead of exceptions
Statically linked single-binary deployment and simple cross-compilation (GOOS/GOARCH)

typing.notes: Named types are nominal and never implicitly converted, but interface satisfaction is structural: any type with the right methods implements an interface without declaring it. `:=` infers local variable types, and type arguments to generic functions are usually inferred.

influenced_by.note: Basic syntax, expressions, pointers (without arithmetic) and the systems-programming niche; Thompson had co-created Unix and C's predecessor B.
Head of the Wirth language line that Donovan & Kernighan call a major stream of influence (declarations, packages).
Wikipedia credits Smalltalk protocols as an inspiration for Go's interfaces.
Listed by Wikipedia; Go's `iota` constant generator takes its name from APL's index generator ι.
Listed by Wikipedia; as in BCPL, line ends can terminate statements, so semicolons rarely appear in source.

The Go FAQ credits the Pascal/Modula/Oberon family with significant input (declarations, packages). Per Donovan & Kernighan, Oberon removed the interface/implementation file split, Oberon-2 shaped package, import and declaration syntax, and Object Oberon supplied the method-receiver syntax. Co-designer Robert Griesemer did his doctorate under Mössenböck and Wirth at ETH Zurich.

influenced_by_external.name: Object Oberon
influenced_by_external.note: Syntax for method declarations with receivers (Donovan & Kernighan).

influenced_by_external.name: Communicating Sequential Processes (Hoare)
influenced_by_external.note: The formal model behind goroutines, channels and `select`.

influenced_by_external.name: Newsqueak
influenced_by_external.note: Rob Pike's concurrent language with first-class channels.

influenced_by_external.name: Alef
influenced_by_external.note: Plan 9 systems language with channels and threads.

influenced_by_external.name: Limbo
influenced_by_external.note: Inferno language Pike worked on: channels, garbage collection, C-like syntax.

influenced_by_external.name: occam
influenced_by_external.note: Listed by Wikipedia among Go's CSP-derived influences.

structured-control.note: `for` is the only loop keyword; `switch` cases do not fall through.

recursion.note: Goroutine stacks grow dynamically; no tail-call elimination.

exceptions.note: `panic`/`recover` exist for truly exceptional cases; ordinary errors are values returned alongside results.

generators.note: Range-over-function iterators: a function taking a `yield` callback can drive a for-range loop (package iter).

type-inference.note: Local only: `x := expr`, plus inference of generic type arguments.

generics.note: Type parameters constrained by interfaces (type sets). Methods may declare their own type parameters only since Go 1.27 (2026), and interface methods still cannot.

structural-typing.note: Only for interfaces: a type satisfies an interface by having its methods, with no `implements` declaration.

interfaces.note: Small, implicitly satisfied interfaces such as io.Reader and io.Writer are the main abstraction mechanism.

traits-mixins.note: Struct embedding promotes the embedded type's methods — composition rather than inheritance.

abstract-data-types.note: Encapsulation is per package: identifiers starting with a lower-case letter are unexported.

modules.note: Packages with explicit imports (unused imports are errors); versioned modules since Go 1.11 (2018).

closures.note: Function literals capture variables by reference; since Go 1.22 each loop iteration gets a fresh variable.

garbage-collection.note: Concurrent, low-pause tri-colour mark-and-sweep collector (concurrent since Go 1.5).

pointers.note: Explicit pointers with & and *, but no pointer arithmetic outside package unsafe, and memory is garbage-collected.

csp-channels.note: `go` statements, typed channels (`chan T`, `<-ch`) and `select` are part of the language.

reflection.note: Runtime reflection via the standard `reflect` package.

regex-builtin.note: Standard `regexp` package (RE2 syntax, linear-time matching); no regex literals.

milestones.event: Griesemer, Pike and Thompson begin designing Go at Google (21 September)
Thompson's prototype compiler; Ian Lance Taylor starts the gccgo front end
Released as open source (10 November); TIOBE's language of the year
Go 1.0 (28 March) with the Go 1 compatibility promise
Go 1.5: compiler and runtime rewritten in Go; concurrent garbage collector
Go 1.22 ranges over integers with per-iteration loop variables; Go 1.23 adds range-over-function iterators
Go 1.27 allows methods to declare their own type parameters (generic methods)

trivia: The gopher mascot was drawn by Renée French, who also designed Glenda, the Plan 9 bunny; it was adapted from a gopher she had drawn for a WFMU T-shirt.
The language is officially just 'Go'; 'golang' comes from the original website domain, golang.org.
On launch day Francis McCabe, author of the older Go! language, asked Google to rename it; the issue was closed in 2010 as 'Unfortunate'.

fizzbuzz.notes: A tagless `switch` replaces an if/else chain; cases never fall through unless marked `fallthrough`.

higher-order.notes: The standard library has no map/filter; a plain loop with `append` remains idiomatic even with generics (1.18) and iterators (1.23).

shapes.notes: Rectangle and Triangle never mention Shape: interface satisfaction is implicit and checked at compile time. Methods can be declared on any named type, not just structs.

signature.title: Goroutines and channels: a concurrent prime sieve
signature.notes: Each `go` statement starts a goroutine; unbuffered channels make sender and receiver rendezvous, CSP-style. Every prime found adds a new filter goroutine to the chain. This sieve is one of the example programs offered on the go.dev playground.

toolchains.name: Go (gc)
toolchains.notes: Verified with golang:1.26-alpine (go1.26.5) and a host go1.27.1. `go run {file}` also works for one-shot runs. plw-go is golang:1.26-alpine with the build cache pre-warmed for common std packages (fmt, strings, sync, time and so on), so a run skips recompiling them.

browser.name: GopherJS Playground
browser.notes: Compiles Go to JavaScript client-side. GopherJS supports Go up to 1.21 (as of mid-2026), so newer language features fail; all six snippets stay within Go 1.21.

runtime.notes: The official go.dev playground compiles on Google's servers, not in the browser.
